This is a blending-appellation wine built on Carignan, Grenache, and likely Syrah or Mourvèdre, sourced from vines old enough to have survived the phylloxera replanting era. parsed.wine_summary:
Domaine Lafage is run by Jean-Marc and Eliane Lafage out of Perpignan, and it's become one of the benchmark estates for showing what Roussillon can do when someone actually pays attention to it. Jean-Marc trained as an oenologist and spent time working harvests across the globe before coming home to the western Mediterranean coast — that technical fluency shows in wines that are clean, focused, and free of the overripe jammy weight that plagued southern French reds for decades.

The Tessellae Old Vines sits in the mid-tier of the Lafage lineup, above their entry-level Cuvée Nicolas but below single-parcel expressions like Clos Codalets. 'Old vines' in Roussillon isn't a marketing fiction — the region has some of the oldest working Carignan in France, with parcels exceeding 80–100 years, and Lafage sources from these for exactly the reason you'd expect: lower yields, more concentrated fruit, deeper mineral character. The appellation rules for Côtes du Roussillon rouge require a blend from at least two of Carignan, Grenache, Lledoner Pelut, Mourvèdre, and Syrah, which means this wine is built for complexity through complementary varieties rather than varietal purity.
parsed.terroir_expression: Roussillon sits in a natural amphitheater formed by the Pyrenees to the south and west, the Corbières massif to the north, and the Mediterranean to the east — a geography that creates one of the driest, sunniest climates in France, averaging around 300 days of sun and under 500mm of annual rainfall. The tramontane wind, a cold dry northwesterly that funnels through the Aude gap, is the key moderating force: it reduces disease pressure dramatically, which is why Roussillon has some of the highest rates of organic and biodynamic farming in France. The schist and gneiss soils that give Tessellae its name are poor, free-draining, and heat-retentive — they radiate warmth back onto the vine canopy at night, extending phenolic ripeness while the tramontane keeps freshness intact. Old Carignan on schist is particularly expressive: the variety's naturally high acidity is preserved by the site's drainage and wind exposure, while the dark volcanic-adjacent mineral quality of the rock shows up as an iron-tinged, graphite-like thread running through the fruit.
parsed.vinification_summary: Lafage uses carbonic or semi-carbonic maceration for at least a portion of the Carignan — a technique where whole uncrushed grapes ferment inside their own skins under CO2, producing wines with brighter fruit, lower harsh tannins, and that distinctive red-fruit-meets-spice character that makes old-vine Carignan so compelling rather than rustic. The Grenache component is almost certainly handled more traditionally with destemming and pump-overs to extract color and structure. Aging is likely in a combination of large foudres (old large-format oak barrels that impart minimal wood character) and possibly some neutral smaller barrique — Lafage's style across the range avoids new oak dominance, keeping the wine's fruit and mineral expression in front. The result is a wine that's technically clean and approachable young but has the structural backbone from Carignan's acidity and Mourvèdre or Syrah's tannin to hold for several years.
parsed.food_pairing:
1. Lamb merguez with harissa and flatbread — the wine's iron-mineral quality and red fruit echo the spiced lamb fat perfectly, and its acidity cuts the richness without fighting the heat. This is a natural pairing rooted in the shared North African culinary influence on Roussillon's food culture.
2. Duck confit with lentils du Puy — the rendered duck fat needs the wine's tannin structure to cleanse the palate, while the earthy lentils mirror the schist-driven mineral thread in the wine.
3. Grilled chistorra sausage with piquillo peppers — chistorra is a fast-cured Basque-Navarran chorizo, and the smoky paprika in it locks onto the wine's dark fruit and any Syrah-derived pepper note. Casual, weeknight, completely correct.
4. Braised short rib with olives and tomatoes — a slow-cooked braise softens the wine's tannins through the fat, and the olive brine and tomato acidity mirror the wine's own savory, medium-acid structure.
5. Aged Manchego with quince paste — for a cheese course, the wine's dried fruit and mineral qualities play off the lanolin and salt of the Manchego, while quince paste bridges the fruit register. Fine dining cheese trolley or a kitchen counter snack — works either way.
parsed.comparable_wines:
Domaine Gauby Vieilles Vignes Rouge, Côtes Catalanes — Gauby farms similar schist soils with old Carignan and Grenache, and while it's a step up in price and intensity, the mineral-driven structure and old-vine concentration are the same argument made at higher volume. Gauby is the benchmark against which Tessellae punches.
Chateau Pech Redon L'Epervier, Coteaux du Languedoc — similar southern French blend profile, similar price range, similar Mediterranean climate influence, but Pech Redon's limestone soils give a rounder, less iron-edged character than Roussillon schist.
Borie La Vitarèle Clos des Martialis, Saint-Chinian — Syrah and Carignan dominant, schist soils, similar tramontane-influenced freshness, and a producer with the same commitment to site expression over extraction. Slightly more Syrah-forward than Tessellae likely is.
parsed.style_profile: Medium-to-full-bodied dry red blend with firm Carignan-driven acidity, moderate tannin, and iron-mineral depth
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink now through 2026–2028 for the 2018 vintage. The wine is approachable on release but the old-vine structure rewards 2–4 years of bottle time, when the tannins soften and the mineral character becomes more defined. Store at 12–14°C away from light.
parsed.value_assessment: Pricing at the LCBO isn't confirmed in the data provided, but comparable Lafage wines in the Tessellae tier typically retail in the $18–$25 CAD range. At that price, the direct competitors are Château Pech Redon and the Gérard Bertrand Réserve Spéciale Languedoc — both decent, both more generic. Tessellae wins on specificity: named soils, old vines, a producer with a trackable house style. It's worth buying.
parsed.market_position: This wine lives on the casual-to-mid-range restaurant list and the everyday retail shelf — it's not a collector's wine and it's not trying to be. The audience is the wine-curious drinker who has moved past entry-level Côtes du Rhône and wants something with more terroir signal without crossing into the $35+ tier. It also works well as a by-the-glass pour at restaurants that want a southern French red with a story that's easy to tell.
parsed.insider_take: Roussillon gets dismissed as Languedoc's rougher cousin, but that's a reading from 20 years ago. The schist soils here produce Carignan with a mineral freshness that Grenache-dominant southern Rhône blends don't have, and Lafage has been one of the producers making that case consistently. The tradeoff with Tessellae specifically is that it's a blended, volume-oriented wine — you're buying the house style and the soil type, not a single parcel. If you want the ceiling of what Roussillon old-vine Carignan can do, Gauby or Clos Codalets is the answer. If you want that argument made accessibly and at a fair price, Tessellae is exactly right.
